name: Fresh Green
lede: Fresh Green is a bright, light spring green, a descriptive name the books use for park plantings and Babar's suit.

sections.title: Leaves and parks
sections.body:
Pastoureau describes the nineteenth-century city park, in which everything was green: delicate or fresh green for the plants and dark or greyish green for the objects, from chairs to bins to the park attendants' uniforms [1]. He also notes that the hero of the Babar books wears a lovely fresh green suit, so that the shade took his name, Babar green [2]. Pastoureau dates the Babar books to the 1930s, from Jean de Brunhoff [2].

St Clair describes the amaranth, a plant with fresh green leaves and dense blooms that never fade, in an Aesop fable [3]. It is a descriptive phrase, near [[lime]] and [[chartreuse]] in the data, not a dated pigment.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: #69D84F is a light, high-chroma green [9]. The books use the words loosely [1][2]. The concordance of 29 color books finds only four strong mentions of this name, so the article stays short rather than pad the record [9]. Screen colors are approximate, and the swatch is a reference value, not a measured pigment [9].
